lessons.title: Matching Strategies to Regimes: A Practical Framework

body.text: A practical framework turns 'lean into momentum when trending' into an actual number you multiply a position size by, not a vague instinct you apply inconsistently.

children.text: The previous lesson diagnosed the problem: unconditioned momentum and mean reversion cancel each other and pay costs for it. This lesson builds the fix as an explicit weighting rule, using the regime probabilities Chapters 2 through 4 already know how to produce.
From Regime Probability to Strategy Weight

Momentum and mean reversion are primarily bets on the trend dimension from Chapter 1, not the volatility dimension. Keep the two separate: a probability of being in a trending regime, P(trend), drives the momentum versus mean-reversion mix in this lesson, however you choose to estimate it, a dedicated trend-focused HMM, a smoothed version of Chapter 2's crossover flag, or Chapter 4's fitted regime mean. The volatility dimension from Chapters 3 and 4 is reserved for overall position sizing, covered properly in Chapter 6. Mixing the two roles into one number is a common design mistake worth avoiding from the start.

body.caption: A linear blend: each strategy's signal is weighted directly by the current trend-regime probability

children.text: When P(trend) is high, momentum dominates the blended signal and mean reversion is nearly switched off, and vice versa. There is no hard cutoff anywhere, which is exactly the point after Chapter 2's lesson on why hard cutoffs whipsaw.
When Neither Strategy Deserves Full Weight

Splitting weight between momentum and mean reversion is not the whole story. When P(trend) sits close to 0.5, the model is genuinely unsure which regime applies, and that uncertainty should shrink total exposure, not just change how it is split. Define confidence as distance from maximum uncertainty.

body.caption: Confidence: 0 when P(trend) = 0.5, the maximum possible uncertainty, rising to 1 as P(trend) approaches 0 or 1

children.text: A simple, illustrative exposure rule scales total capital deployed from half size at zero confidence up to full size at maximum confidence: total exposure = 0.5 + 0.5 x confidence. This is one reasonable starting rule among many, refined properly once Chapter 6 covers capital allocation across regimes in full.

body.caption: The framework applied to Chapter 1's four regime archetypes (illustrative P(trend) values)

body.text: Notice what happens to Volatile Whipsaw: it does not get a clean momentum-versus-reversion split like the other three archetypes, it gets the lowest confidence and the lowest total exposure scalar of all four. That is the framework correctly recognizing what Chapter 1 argued qualitatively: this regime is genuinely hard for both strategies, and the right response is smaller size for everyone, not a clever way to pick a winner between momentum and mean reversion.

children.text: Also notice Panic Selloff still gives momentum the higher weight, 0.70. That reflects a real, well-known piece of practitioner judgment: during a confirmed, trending decline, momentum, meaning short exposure that bets on continuation, tends to fare better than early mean reversion, meaning buying the dip on the assumption of an imminent bounce. Bottom-fishing too early in a genuine panic is one of the classic ways mean-reversion strategies lose money.

body.text: These weights and exposure scalars are a starting framework, not a validated trading rule. Every number in this lesson's table was chosen to illustrate the mechanics clearly, not fitted or backtested. Chapter 7 covers exactly the discipline needed before any version of this framework should be trusted with real capital.

body.title: Computing Confidence and Exposure
body.prompt: P(trend) for a given day is 0.30. Using confidence = 2 x |P(trend) - 0.5| and total exposure = 0.5 + 0.5 x confidence, what is the total exposure scalar?
body.explanation: confidence = 2 x |0.30 - 0.50| = 2 x 0.20 = 0.40. Total exposure = 0.5 + 0.5 x 0.40 = 0.5 + 0.20 = 0.70. Note the mean-reversion weight here would be 1 - 0.30 = 0.70, the same number as the exposure scalar by coincidence at this particular P(trend) value, not because the two formulas are related.

body.title: Applying the Framework to a New Regime Reading
body.scenario: Your fitted regime model reports P(trend) = 0.58 for Nifty today, meaningfully above 0.5 but far from the 0.85 seen in a clean Calm Uptrend.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's framework, what momentum weight, mean-reversion weight, confidence, and total exposure scalar does this produce, and how would you describe this regime in plain terms compared to the four archetypes in the table?
body.modelAnswer: Momentum weight = 0.58, mean-reversion weight = 1 - 0.58 = 0.42. Confidence = 2 x |0.58 - 0.50| = 0.16, and total exposure = 0.5 + 0.5 x 0.16 = 0.58. This sits well below every archetype in the table on confidence, closer to Volatile Whipsaw's 0.10 than to any of the clearer regimes, even though the raw P(trend) value is not extreme. In plain terms, this looks like a mildly trending market where the evidence for a real trend is weak, closer to a coin flip than a conviction call, so both strategies get modest weight and the desk should be running meaningfully reduced size until the signal firms up in either direction.

points: Momentum versus mean-reversion weighting should be driven by the trend dimension specifically, kept separate from the volatility dimension, which drives overall sizing in Chapter 6
A simple linear blend, weighting momentum by P(trend) and mean reversion by 1 - P(trend), replaces a hard switch with a continuous mix that avoids Chapter 2's whipsaw problem
Confidence, 2 x |P(trend) - 0.5|, captures how far the model is from maximum uncertainty and should scale total exposure, not just the split between strategies
Applied to Chapter 1's four archetypes, Volatile Whipsaw correctly receives the lowest confidence and lowest total exposure, matching the qualitative warning from Chapter 1
This framework's specific numbers are illustrative starting points; Chapter 7's backtesting discipline is required before trusting any version of it with real capital
